text: Before anything else. Every other page on this site shows you something that has been measured. This one has not. That is what the speculative badge means, and I am going to keep saying it.

The other thing worth knowing up front is that multiverse is three completely different ideas wearing one word. They come from different physics, they claim different things, and people argue past each other constantly because of it.

The first one. Inflation is the enormous burst of expansion in the first instant of the universe, and it is well motivated — it fits the microwave background well. The awkward part is that in most versions, inflation never actually stops.
It keeps going almost everywhere, and bubbles of ordinary, non-inflating space appear inside it. Each bubble is a universe. Ours is one of them.

Now watch the gap between them. The space in between is inflating faster than the bubbles grow into it, so two bubbles are moving apart faster than light can cross the distance. Nothing will ever get from one to the other.
That is not a technological problem. There is no signal, no particle and no observation that can ever pass between them. Which is precisely why this is hard to call science in the usual sense.
The second idea is completely unrelated, and it comes from quantum mechanics.

Quantum mechanics says an unmeasured particle is in several states at once, and measuring it gives you just one. Many worlds says the other outcomes do not disappear. Every measurement splits reality, and you go on down one branch without noticing.

Here is the honest part. Many worlds makes exactly the same predictions as every other interpretation for every experiment ever done. That is not a criticism, it is the definition of an interpretation — but it means no experiment can currently tell them apart.
The third comes from string theory.

Every valley in this landscape is a different stable configuration, and each one has its own physical constants. Different electron mass, different strength of gravity, different everything. The blue marker is ours.

The usual estimate for the number of valleys is ten to the five hundred. That is not a big number, that is an absurd number — far more than the atoms in the observable universe, squared, several times over.
And that is the real objection, for all three. Look at the row that asks whether there is any way to test it.

A theory that can accommodate any observation predicts nothing. The serious complaint about the multiverse is not that it is strange. It is that no measurement we could make would come out differently if it were false.

There is one genuine exception, and it is worth knowing. If our bubble collided with a neighbour early on, it would have left a circular cold or warm disc in the microwave background. People have looked. Nothing convincing has turned up — but that is a real, falsifiable test, and it is the only one on this page.
So: three interesting ideas that fall out of theories that work well elsewhere, and no evidence for any of them. Untested is not the same as false, and it is not the same as true either.
